disputes: Body without organs in The Logic of Sense, as shown on the entry (re-read 2026-11-19 against SEP §3.2 and LOS series 27): Intensities in The Logic of Sense? The Stanford Encyclopedia article (revised by Daniela Voss, 2022) reads the book as calling the newborn's “life of intensities-in-motion” the body without organs, and pictures that life with Daniel Stern's image of infant experience, published in 1985. The Stanford article and the book both place the body without organs in the infant: the book sets it in the infant's schizoid position, Klein's position as Deleuze revises it (pp. 187–188), to which, it supposes, the schizophrenic regresses (p. 189), the schizophrenic whose body without organs is Artaud's glorious body (pp. 88, 90). They part only on “intensities”, which the book's pages on it never use. The book gives intensity to the erogenous zones of the surface (p. 225), and its essay on Klossowski calls breaths “pure intensities” (p. 297), a possible bridge. The article says Deleuze draws on “a tradition of developmental psychology” and gives Stern's image as its expression; the intensity wording in that paragraph is Stern's, published sixteen years after the book. Not settled.

Sense-event, “sterile division” or “decoupling”: Sterile division or decoupling? Lester and Stivale translate Deleuze's dédoublement as “sterile division” (p. 31). James Williams translates it “decoupling”, since French has its own word, division, and Deleuze avoids it in this passage: on his reading the paradox cuts a single dry proposition loose from the regress, and its sense drifts off sterile (Williams, p. 55). He also reads the two paradoxes as relaunching each other, so that the alternative between them keeps sense in movement (Williams, p. 55).

Aion-chronos, the present (Badiou and Williams): The present: as James Williams reports it, Alain Badiou, in Logiques des mondes (2006; translated as Logics of Worlds), centres time and ethics on the present, where a subject incorporates into the present of a truth. James Williams calls this a moral “presentism” and argues that Deleuze's two presents answer it: the present of Chronos, where the event strikes the body, and the present of the actor, which counter-actualizes it (p. 168), with eternal ideas working on every present because they are neutral and impassive (Williams, pp. 172–174). Badiou's book has not been read for this entry; his position is given as Williams reports it.

Counter-actualization, guidance for action (open question): Can counter-actualization guide action? James Williams asks whether its principles are too abstract for specific wrongs and too individualistic for an ethics that begins from living with others (Williams, p. 153), and whether replaying events suits an age that can cure and prevent what it once had to bear (Williams, p. 158). He takes up the first question again through the series on the Aion and on univocity (Williams, pp. 169–174); the entry leaves the questions open.

new_d.text: Deleuze's account, in The Logic of Sense (1969), of sense as a fourth dimension of the proposition: an incorporeal event that subsists in propositions and is attributed to things, at the boundary between the two.

new_text.text: Deleuze presents The Logic of Sense as a series of paradoxes that form the theory of sense, with a privileged place for Lewis Carroll, who first staged those paradoxes, and for the Stoics, who began a new image of what a philosopher is (p. xiii), and calls it an attempt at “a logical and psychological novel” (p. xiv).
Pages of The Logic of Sense are from the translation by Mark Lester with Charles Stivale, edited by Constantin V. Boundas (1990).
He starts from the Stoic division of things into two kinds (pp. 4–5).

On one side are bodies, with their qualities, actions and passions and the states of affairs they make up, which are causes for one another; on the other are the incorporeal effects of these causes, “logical or dialectical attributes” of which one can only say that they “subsist or inhere” (p. 5).
When a scalpel cuts flesh, Émile Bréhier writes in a passage Deleuze quotes, it produces in the flesh a new attribute, being cut, which leaves its properties as they were (p. 5).
Deleuze sets green, a quality of the mixture that tree and air make, beside “to green”, an attribute said of the tree (pp. 6, 21).

Three relations within the proposition are commonly recognized, he writes (pp. 12–15): denotation, its relation to a state of affairs, judged true or false; manifestation, its relation to the person who speaks, with that person's desires and beliefs; and signification, its relation to general concepts and to the propositions that imply it or that it implies.
Each in turn grounds or presupposes another, so that they form what he calls the circle of the proposition (pp. 16–17).
Sense is a fourth dimension (p. 19): what the proposition expresses, an “incorporeal, complex, and irreducible entity, at the surface of things” (p. 19).

Deleuze credits its discovery to the Stoics, and finds it again in the fourteenth century in Gregory of Rimini and Nicholas of Autrecourt and at the end of the nineteenth in Meinong (p. 19); Husserl's name for it is expression (p. 20).
Sense has no existence outside the proposition that expresses it, yet it belongs as an attribute to the thing or state of affairs, while a proposition's own attribute is its predicate (p. 21).

It is “exactly the boundary between propositions and things” (p. 22), and Deleuze identifies it with the event: “the event is sense itself” (p. 22), so long as the event is kept apart from the state of affairs that realizes it (p. 22).
The fifth series sets out the paradoxes of sense (pp. 28–35).

The sense of what I say can be stated only in another proposition, whose sense needs a further one, a regress Deleuze calls Frege's paradox and also Carroll's (pp. 28–29); sense suspends affirmation and negation, so that “God is” and “God is not” have the same sense (pp. 31–33); and propositions about impossible objects such as square circles have a sense and no signification, so the absurd and nonsense must be kept apart (p. 35).

The second, the paradox of sterile division, arises when the sense of a proposition is extracted as a neutralized double of it (p. 31), and sets a task for later: to “combine the sterility of sense” with “its power of genesis” with respect to the proposition's dimensions (p. 32).

Sense, he argues, is produced by nonsense: a paradoxical element, always displaced and absent from its own place, which appears in one series as an empty square (p. 51), circulates through both series and produces sense in each as an effect (pp. 70–71).

He credits the authors called structuralists with this view of sense as a surface effect and a position effect (p. 71), and welcomes the news “that sense is never a principle or an origin” and is produced (p. 72).
Events bear on problems and define their conditions: “The mode of the event is the problematic” (p. 54).
The fourteenth series takes up that task (pp. 94–99).
Sense results from bodies and their mixtures, and so is always in danger of being “snapped up by its cause” (p. 94).
Following the Stoics, Deleuze gives the event a “double causality” (p. 94): bodies are its cause, and other events its quasi-cause.
The quasi-cause is the paradoxical element of nonsense, which secures “the full autonomy of the effect” (p. 95).

Taken as the effect of bodies, sense is impassible and sterile; taken together with the quasi-cause, it shares in that cause's force and becomes productive, engendering the dimensions of the proposition and what fulfils them: states of affairs, states of the subject, concepts and classes (pp. 95–96).
Deleuze calls “the passage from sterility to genesis” the problem the logic of sense always returns to (p. 97).

Husserl, on his account, found sense impassible again in the noema, and then made its genesis depend on common sense, good sense and the form of a person (pp. 96–98); a genesis of sense needs an impersonal transcendental field, the condition Deleuze takes from Sartre's article of 1937 (pp. 98–99), determined by singularities (p. 99).
The static genesis (series 15–17) shows how sense produces what the circle of the proposition took as given: individuals, persons and concepts, and the proposition's dimensions.
Singularities, impersonal and pre-individual, are distributed over a surface, and Deleuze calls them “the true transcendental events” (pp. 102–103).

In the ontological genesis a world forms where the series around singularities converge, and individuals are constituted in it, each enveloping a finite number of its singularities (pp. 109–110); Leibniz's compossibility is the rule of this convergence, and where series diverge an incompossible world begins (p. 111).
On a second level persons appear: a “thing = x common to several worlds”, such as a “vague Adam” (p. 114), defined by synthetic predicates, from which classes and properties derive (p. 115).
The first stage, he writes, is “the work of sense”, the second “the work of nonsense” (p. 116).

In the logical genesis, denotation relates the proposition to individuals, manifestation to persons, and signification to the classes and properties that depend on persons, though Deleuze denies any simple parallel between the two geneses (pp. 118–119); sense is “doubly generative” (p. 120), engendering the proposition and the things its dimensions bear on.
Sense is then expressed as a problem, which propositions answer (pp. 120–121).

The idea of a static genesis, he writes, resolves the contradiction between sterility and genesis (p. 124): bodies produce sense from their depth by forming surfaces, and sense, once at the surface, shares in the quasi-cause and in turn produces individuation and signification (pp. 124–126).

James Williams, in his guide to the book (2008), calls the quasi-cause one of Deleuze's rare “heavy and clumsy concepts”, resting on stretched analogies with the physics of surfaces, and then defends it: on his reading the quasi-cause changes the relation of actual things to sense and leaves their measurable properties alone (Williams, p. 130).

He glosses “static” through the French physique statique, “the physics of things in equilibrium”, and reads genesis as the emergence of what is singular, and so open to change, in things already identified (Williams, pp. 124–125); the static genesis works, he writes, by limitation (Williams, p. 126).
He warns against taking sense for meaning: meaning changes with each proposition, and sense stays neutral across them (Williams, p. 56).

Pages of Williams are from his Gilles Deleuze's Logic of Sense: A Critical Introduction and Guide (Edinburgh University Press, 2008); they are pages of the guide and open nothing in your copy of Deleuze.

new_d.text: The two readings of time in Deleuze's The Logic of Sense (1969): Chronos, in which only the present exists, and Aion, in which only past and future subsist and divide every present without end.

new_text.text: Deleuze takes the pair from the Stoics, for whom, he writes, time must be grasped twice: entirely as the living present of bodies that act and are acted on, and entirely as divisible without end into past and future, “two simultaneous readings of time” (p. 5).
Pages of The Logic of Sense are from the translation by Mark Lester with Charles Stivale, edited by Constantin V. Boundas (1990).

In Chronos only the present exists, and past and future are relative to a present: what is past or future for one present belongs to a vaster one, up to the divine present of the whole cosmos (pp. 162–163).
It is the time of bodies and their mixtures, and the present measures what bodies and causes do (p. 162).
The time of the present is “a limited but infinite time”, infinite because it is cyclical (p. 61).
Beneath the measured present Deleuze places a becoming-mad of the depths that subverts it, which he calls a bad Chronos (pp. 163–164).
In Aion the past and the future subsist or inhere, and the instant, “without thickness and without extension”, divides each present into past and future in both directions at once (p. 164).
Aion is “a pure straight line at the surface” (p. 62) and the “eternal truth of time” (p. 165).

It is the time of events and effects (p. 62): the event is always at once “something which has just happened and something about to happen” (p. 63), and of dying Deleuze writes that no one ever dies, and one “has always just died or is always going to die” (p. 63).

He lists the contrasts in the twenty-third series (p. 165): Chronos is limited and infinite, circular, and filled entirely by the bodies that are its causes and matter; Aion is unlimited as past and future are, finite as the instant is, a straight line, and haunted by incorporeal effects that never fill it.
Aion traces the frontier between things and propositions, and in this way makes language possible (pp. 166–167).

On its line Deleuze places an eternal return of pure events, set against the circular return of Chronos (p. 176), and borrows from Borges the image of a labyrinth made of a single straight line (pp. 62, 176).
Aion has a present of its own, the present of “the actor, dancer, or mime” (p. 168), and the pure infinitive of the verb, he writes, is the Aion (pp. 184–185).

James Williams reads Aion and Chronos as two incompatible times that determine each other, and the theory as depending on never folding them into one time: the event has “an actual passing side” in Chronos and “an eternal but differential side” in Aion, which is how events can be “both eternal and passing” (Williams, pp. 122–123).

He reads the present of the actor that closes the twenty-third series (p. 168) as Deleuze's answer, decades in advance, to an ethics centred on the present act, of the kind Alain Badiou sets out in Logiques des mondes (2006) (Williams, pp. 172–174).

Pages of Williams are from his Gilles Deleuze's Logic of Sense: A Critical Introduction and Guide (Edinburgh University Press, 2008); they are pages of the guide and open nothing in your copy of Deleuze.

aion-chronos.s: The Logic of Sense (1969), trans. Mark Lester with Charles Stivale (1990), series 2 (pp. 4–11), 10, “Of the Ideal Game” (pp. 58–65), and 23, “Of the Aion” (pp. 162–168); James Williams, Gilles Deleuze's Logic of Sense: A Critical Introduction and Guide (2008)

new_d.text: In Deleuze's The Logic of Sense (1969), the operation that doubles an event's actualization in bodies and states of affairs, modeled on the actor, and draws out the event's impersonal part and its eternal truth.

new_text.text: Every event, Deleuze writes, has a double structure (pp. 151–152): on one side the moment it is actualized, embodied in a person, an individual or a state of affairs; on the other its past and future taken in themselves, impersonal and pre-individual, whose only present is the mobile instant that represents it, which he calls the counter-actualization (p. 151).
He credits Maurice Blanchot with showing this double structure in death, which is grounded in me and my body and also has “no relation to me at all” (p. 151).
Pages of The Logic of Sense are from the translation by Mark Lester with Charles Stivale, edited by Constantin V. Boundas (1990).
Deleuze ties this double structure to ethics: only the free man, he writes, grasps the event and enacts its counter-actualization, and so escapes ressentiment (p. 152).

Stoic ethics, Deleuze writes, consists in willing the event as such, whatever occurs insofar as it occurs (p. 143); he later narrows the formula, so that the will wills “something in that which occurs”, which he calls the Event (p. 149).

Ethics either makes no sense at all, he writes, or it means “not to be unworthy of what happens to us” (p. 149); to take what happens as unjust and as someone else's fault is ressentiment, and resignation, he suggests, is one more figure of it (p. 149).
His example is Joe Bousquet, who took the wound he bore as a pure event (p. 148); events, Deleuze writes, signal to us: “My wound existed before me, I was born to embody it” (p. 148).
The model is the actor (pp. 147, 150).
The actor occupies the instant and plays a role that is always still to come and already past, and so keeps from the event “only its contour and its splendor” (p. 150).

Counter-actualization alone, Deleuze warns, belongs to a buffoon; doubling the event's real actualization, as the true actor and dancer do, it gives the truth of the event “the only chance of not being confused with its inevitable actualization” (p. 161).

In the twenty-second series, which opens on F. Scott Fitzgerald's The Crack-Up, he asks whether one can stop at an event's counter-actualization and prevent its full actualization in the body (p. 157), and answers that the event's eternal truth is grasped only when the event is “also inscribed in the flesh” (p. 161).
Psychoanalysis, the science of pure events in his account, is also, he writes, an art of counter-actualizations (p. 212).

James Williams reads counter-actualization as a replay of the event that leaves its outcome as it was and changes its tone and significance, as Joe Bousquet did with his wound in his books (Williams, p. 155).
He renders Deleuze's amor fati as a “love of the event”, which selects something to affirm on the event's ideal side and neither denies nor resents what happened in the body (Williams, p. 156).

Pages of Williams are from his Gilles Deleuze's Logic of Sense: A Critical Introduction and Guide (Edinburgh University Press, 2008); they are pages of the guide and open nothing in your copy of Deleuze.

summary: Three new entries read in The Logic of Sense (Lester and Stivale's translation), every quotation verbatim and every page checked: sense and event, Aion and Chronos, and counter-actualization. They describe what the book says and credit no one else's reading, since the encyclopedias could not be fetched and Williams's guide was lost; both are listed as unread.
